newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian shares dip 1.25 percent as golds dive.
newsitem.headline: Australian shares dip 1.25 percent as golds dive.

text.p: Tumbling Australian gold stocks set off a 1.25 percent share market fall on Tuesday, which some dealers said could be the start of a downward correction from an 18 percent rally over the past three months.
"The market has had a very strong run in recent months and quite a few valuations were looking a bit expensive," said John Banos, equity strategist at Merrill Lynch Australia.
The key All Ordinaries index ended 33.8 points down at 2,679.2 in moderate overall turnover of A$715 million (US%529 million).

The gold share index plunged another 6.4 percent. Today's dive in the wake of new 12-year lows overnight in bullion prices brings the sector's fall to 16.5 percent since last week's news that the Reserve Bank of Australia had sold two-thirds of its gold reserves.

Gold heavyweight Normandy Mining fell four cents to A$1.28, its lowest levels in over four years while the smaller Acacia Resources fell 15 cents to A$1.30, the lowest level since its listing on the stock exchange.
"Nothing is being saved from the massacre at the moment," one senior dealer said, adding investors were bound to start stock-picking in the sector sometime soon.
Among major gold stocks, Newcrest Mining shed as much as 12.5 percent to A$2.64 and Lihir Gold five percent to A$1.84.
Gold may have been at the top of the agenda, but there were few exceptions to the negative trend among blue chips as declines outnumbered advances by more than five to one.
The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd fell 39.5 cents to end well below A$19 dollars at A$18.855, while WMC lost 30 cents to A$7.84 and Rio Tinto 39 cents to A$22.06.
The interest rate sensitive banks ended mixed. Dealers said there was uncertainty over when another rate cut could happen.
"A cut is still hanging out there, but it's not at the top of people's mind at the moment," one Brisbane-based dealer said.
National Australia Bank closed unchanged at A$19.40 while ANZ fell three cents to A$9.80.

Some dealers said the market is not fundamentally overvalued and that a correction of around five percent from the record high of 2,757.9 on July 3 could provide new buying opportunities. The All Ordinaries has fallen 3.1 percent since then.
"If it goes more than (five percent) I'd argue that you're in relatively cheap territory," equity strategist David Rees of Bankers Trust said.
